lessons.title: Why do we watch films?
lessons.subtitle: Films can entertain us, teach us, and help us see other lives.
sections: Why people watch

People watch films for many reasons: to enjoy a story, laugh, feel suspense, learn about the world or see another person’s point of view. Not every film tells a fictional story; documentaries can show real people and events.
How a film makes us feel

Imagine someone waiting for a friend who does not arrive. The story can be told in one sentence. A film might show an empty chair, a passing train and the person checking the time. Images, timing, acting and sound help us experience the wait.
People may feel different things

Two people can watch the same scene and react differently. Their experiences and expectations can shape what they notice. Filmmakers can guide feelings, but cannot guarantee one reaction from everyone.
lessons.idea: Films can show events and ideas while using images, sound and timing to shape our experience.
lessons.try: Watch a short scene. What did you notice first: a person, an action, a sound or a feeling?
lessons.q: Which choice best describes what cinema can do?
opts: Only communicate facts
Shape how we experience a story
Make every viewer feel exactly the same
lessons.feedback: Images, sound, acting and editing can influence how we feel. Different viewers may still react differently.

lessons.title: How did cinema begin?
lessons.subtitle: Moving pictures developed through many inventions and storytellers.
sections: Before the movie theatre
In the 1800s, inventors explored ways to capture and display movement. Early viewers sometimes watched short moving pictures through individual viewing machines rather than on a large screen.
Pictures for an audience

On 28 December 1895, the Lumière family’s Cinématographe had a famous paid screening in Paris. This was a major moment, but not the very first moving-picture exhibition; other inventors showed moving images earlier.
From invention to storytelling

Early films included everyday events, staged comedy and imaginative tricks. Film developed into many kinds of art and entertainment across countries. History is more than one invention or one country.
lessons.idea: Cinema developed through the work of many people and changed as technology and storytelling changed.
lessons.try: Imagine showing someone a moving picture for the first time. What real moment would you record?
lessons.q: Which statement about early cinema is most accurate?
opts: One person invented every part of cinema
Many people helped develop moving-picture technology and filmmaking
All the earliest films were feature-length fiction
lessons.feedback: Moving images, cameras, projection and film storytelling developed through contributions from many inventors and artists.

lessons.title: Frame, shot, scene
lessons.subtitle: Three common terms every beginner should know.
sections: Frame: one picture
Pause a video. The single image you see is a frame. What appears inside its edges—including people, objects and light—is part of its composition (how the picture is arranged).
Shot: one continuous view
In a finished film, a shot is one uninterrupted view before the film changes to another shot. The camera can stay still or move during it. One shot contains many frames (individual pictures).
Scene: one part of the action

A scene is a part of the story, often in one place and around one stretch of time. It may use one shot or several shots. A take is one attempt to record a shot; filmmakers may record several takes and choose one when editing.
lessons.idea: Frame = one picture. Shot = one continuous view. Scene = one part of the story. Take = one recording attempt.
lessons.try: Watch a short conversation. Count how often the image cuts to another shot. Is it still one scene?
lessons.q: An argument is filmed in one unbroken take and shown without edits. How many shots do we see?
opts: One shot
Always ten shots
One shot per line of dialogue
lessons.feedback: One unbroken take shown without edits is one shot, even if it covers a whole scene.

lessons.title: What kinds of films exist?
lessons.subtitle: Comedy, horror, documentary and many more—often mixed together.
sections: What is a genre?

A genre is a way of grouping stories with shared features. Comedy often aims to amuse; horror often explores fear; a mystery invites us to ask questions. Genres are useful descriptions, not fixed rules.
One film can fit several groups
A film can be funny and scary at once. A romantic drama may also have musical numbers. The same film can be described differently by different viewers and distributors.
Fiction and documentary

Fictional films usually use invented or dramatized events. Documentaries explore actual people, events or issues, but still involve choices about filming and editing. A documentary is not automatically an unbiased record.
lessons.idea: Genre labels help describe what a film offers; they do not limit what filmmakers may create.
lessons.q: Which statement about film genres is accurate?
opts: Every film must belong to exactly one genre
Genres can overlap within one film
Only fictional movies have genres
lessons.feedback: Genres are flexible descriptions. Films often combine elements from several genres.
lessons.try: Invent a story about somebody losing a phone. How could it become a comedy—or a mystery?

lessons.title: How did cinema grow in India?
lessons.subtitle: A short introduction to a long, multilingual filmmaking history.
sections: Early screenings and films

Moving pictures were shown in Bombay (now Mumbai) in 1896. Indian filmmakers were soon experimenting with their own films. Early Indian cinema was silent: it did not have recorded dialogue synchronized to the image.
Two important early milestones

Shree Pundalik (1912) is part of discussions about early Indian feature films. Dadasaheb Phalke’s Raja Harishchandra (1913) is widely recognized as a foundational Indian feature. Calling one film the very first without explanation hides a real historical debate.
Many languages and traditions

Cinema developed across India in many languages and regions. Later, synchronized sound, music, colour, changing film technologies and digital tools opened more ways to tell stories. No single industry represents all Indian filmmaking.
lessons.idea: Indian cinema has a shared history and many distinct regional filmmaking traditions.
lessons.q: What is a careful way to describe early Indian cinema?
opts: It began with only one uncontested first film
It developed through several filmmakers and includes debated early milestones
Every Indian film has always used recorded dialogue
lessons.feedback: Early Indian cinema has multiple contributors. Some first-film claims are debated by historians.
lessons.try: Ask someone in your family about a film they loved when they were young. What felt different from films today?

lessons.title: How stories create emotion
lessons.subtitle: Expectation, surprise and character choices turn events into drama.
sections: Give the character a reason

Imagine someone searching for a key. Now imagine that the key opens a box holding their mother’s last letter. The search matters more because we understand what the person could lose. This is what storytellers mean by the stakes.
Make us wonder what happens next
When a character wants something, we start asking: will they get it? A problem or delay can make us more curious. Waiting for an important answer can create suspense.
Show what someone decides
A character who is afraid to open a letter might put it away, then pick it up again. We can learn about the character from what they do, even without a speech.
lessons.idea: We often care more when we know what a character wants, why it matters and what they choose to do.
lessons.try: Write one sentence: ‘Someone wants ___, but ___ stands in the way.’
lessons.q: Why does a simple problem become compelling drama?
opts: Because it has more camera angles
Because it matters to someone and creates meaningful stakes
Because the scene uses loud music
lessons.feedback: A problem can feel more important when we understand why it matters to a person.

lessons.title: From idea to screenplay
lessons.subtitle: Turn a simple idea into actions that can be filmed.
sections: Begin with someone doing something
An idea could be: “A student finds a lost notebook.” Ask who the student is, what they want to do and what might make the choice difficult.
Write what an audience can notice

A screenplay often describes visible actions, sounds, locations and dialogue. Instead of only saying “she feels nervous,” write something the audience could notice, such as “she hesitates before opening the notebook.”
Keep a first scene small
Try one location, one or two characters and a clear situation. A screenplay is a plan that can change during rehearsal, filming or editing.
lessons.idea: A screenplay gives the filmmaking team a practical way to turn story ideas into scenes.
lessons.try: Write three sentences: who is here, what do they want, and what action shows their problem?
lessons.q: Which line gives filmmakers a clear, filmable action?
opts: The room has a mysterious feeling
She pauses, then hides the letter under a book
It should become an award-winning scene
lessons.feedback: A visible action gives actors and filmmakers something concrete to interpret and film.

lessons.title: How performance tells a story
lessons.subtitle: Small choices in action and voice can reveal a character.
sections: Acting is more than dialogue
An actor can communicate through looking, moving, pausing, breathing and speaking. None of these has one universal meaning; the situation matters.
Give an action a purpose
A character may want to apologize but struggle to begin. A pause or a change in eye contact may help show that difficulty, if it fits the performance.
A performance works with the frame
A close-up can make subtle facial details easier to notice. A wide shot can let us notice a person’s movement in a space. The camera and edit help shape what we see of the performance.
lessons.idea: Performance communicates through choices in action, expression, movement and voice.
lessons.try: Say “I am here” once as a happy greeting, once as a worried announcement. Notice what changes beyond the words.
lessons.q: Which can help communicate a character’s feelings?
opts: Only spoken words
Actions, voice, movement and expression
A camera angle without any other context
lessons.feedback: Acting can communicate through many kinds of behavior, not only dialogue.

lessons.title: Characters, wants and obstacles
lessons.subtitle: Understand what makes even a tiny story interesting.
sections: What does the character want?
A character might want a train ticket, an apology, a moment of quiet or simply to get home. A want can give us a direction to follow. Not every film follows one main character.
What gets in the way?
An obstacle may be another person, a situation, a rule or the character’s own fear. Conflict in storytelling does not always mean shouting or fighting.
Why does the choice matter?
If the person misses the bus, will they lose a job interview—or just wait ten minutes? The consequences of a choice are sometimes called the stakes. Small stakes can still feel meaningful.
lessons.idea: A simple way to begin a story is to ask what a character wants, what makes it difficult and what they choose.
lessons.q: In a story, an obstacle can be...
opts: Only a villain
Only a physical fight
An external problem or an internal fear
lessons.feedback: An obstacle can come from the world around a character or from within the character.
lessons.try: Write: “A person wants ____, but ____. They decide to ____.”

lessons.title: Dialogue: more than words
lessons.subtitle: What characters say—and what they avoid saying.
sections: Dialogue is spoken language
Dialogue is what characters say. The meaning of a line can depend on voice, the relationship between speakers and what happens around them. A scene can also tell a story with little or no dialogue.
Meaning beneath the words
A character says, “You’re early,” but avoids eye contact. Perhaps the words are polite while the action suggests discomfort. This possible unstated meaning is often called subtext.
Make words useful
Words can reveal information, character or conflict. But do not make a character explain what viewers already understand from action unless that repetition serves a purpose.
lessons.idea: Dialogue, action, silence and performance work together; the words alone are rarely the whole scene.
lessons.q: What is subtext?
opts: A subtitle shown at the bottom of a film
A possible meaning implied rather than said directly
Every sentence in a screenplay
lessons.feedback: Subtext is a possible underlying meaning suggested by context, performance or what remains unsaid.
lessons.try: Write two ways to say “I’m fine.” How could the actor show different meanings?

lessons.title: Show a feeling through action
lessons.subtitle: Help the audience notice an idea rather than only hearing an explanation.
sections: What can the audience actually see?

A character says, “I miss my friend.” That tells us the feeling in words. Or the character may set out two cups, then put one away. The action gives viewers something to observe and interpret. Neither approach is automatically better.
Show and tell can work together

A film may use dialogue, action, performance, images and sound together. A character might say one thing while their actions suggest another. Good dialogue does not need to be removed just because an action could tell part of the story.
Choose the clearest approach

Ask: what should the audience know now, and what should they discover later? If a visual clue is too vague, a short line of dialogue may help. If the action already makes something clear, repeating it in words may be unnecessary.
lessons.idea: Showing is one storytelling choice, not a ban on explanation or dialogue.
lessons.try: Write two versions of a tiny moment: one as dialogue, one as visible action. What does each reveal?
lessons.q: Which statement about “show, don’t tell” is best?
opts: Every line of dialogue makes a film worse
Visible action and dialogue can both communicate story information
A character must never explain anything
lessons.feedback: A filmmaker can choose action, dialogue, or both depending on the scene.

lessons.title: What makes a shot good?
lessons.subtitle: A good shot helps the viewer see or feel what matters.
sections: Pretty is not the same as useful
A shot can look beautiful but still distract us from an important moment. Ask what the audience should notice in this part of the film.
Know what you want to show
Do viewers need to see the whole place, two people together or one small facial reaction? Choose what goes inside the frame and how you show it to support that idea.
One shot can mean different things

A wide shot shows more of the surroundings. It might suggest loneliness—or freedom. A close-up shows detail, such as a face. It might feel warm, funny or uncomfortable. The story and nearby shots help give each choice meaning.
lessons.idea: A shot works well when it helps communicate what matters in that moment.
lessons.try: Open the Creative Lab and compare the same character in three shot sizes. Choose a framing for a lonely character. Explain why you picked it.
lessons.q: What is the best first question to ask when choosing a shot?
opts: Which lens looks most expensive?
What does this scene need the audience to experience?
Can every shot be a close-up?
lessons.feedback: First decide what viewers need to see or feel. Then choose how to frame and film it.

lessons.title: Where should the camera go?
lessons.subtitle: Distance and angle subtly change your relationship to a character.
sections: Where the camera sits matters
The camera’s position changes what fits in the picture and which details we notice. Moving closer or farther away can change how we see a person and their surroundings.
High and low angles
Filming someone from below can make them seem large or important. Filming from above may make them seem small. But neither angle has one fixed meaning; the scene decides how we read it.
Move the camera for a reason
A moving camera can follow a person or reveal something new. A still camera can let us study what happens. Both are useful; decide what viewers should notice.
lessons.idea: Ask what you want the viewer to see before choosing a camera position or movement.
lessons.try: Place your phone at eye level, knee height and above eye level. Take three photos of the same object. Compare the feelings.
lessons.q: What gives a low camera angle meaning?
opts: It always means heroism
The specific scene, subject and surrounding choices
It always makes a scene better
lessons.feedback: The meaning of a camera angle depends on the subject, the framing and the scene.

lessons.title: What does lighting do?
lessons.subtitle: Light helps us see faces, shapes, spaces and details.
sections: Light makes things visible
Where a light comes from, its size and brightness affect the highlights and shadows we see. A big nearby light source can create softer-looking shadows than a small source, all else being equal.
Look at the direction
A front light may reveal more of a face. A side light can show differences in brightness across it. A backlight can separate a subject from the background with an edge of light.
No automatic emotion
Darkness is not always scary. Brightness is not always happy. Lighting works with story, acting, camera and design.
lessons.idea: Lighting shapes visibility and contrast, giving filmmakers ways to direct attention.
lessons.try: Use the Lighting Lab, then compare the effect using a safe desk lamp and a still object.
lessons.q: What affects how lighting looks on a face?
opts: Only the price of the camera
Light direction, size, distance and strength
One lighting arrangement always means one emotion
lessons.feedback: Several properties of the light and the scene affect its appearance; no emotional effect is guaranteed.

lessons.title: Arrange the frame
lessons.subtitle: Guide attention through placement, space and visual contrast.
sections: What belongs in the image?
Composition means arranging visual elements inside the frame. A person near the edge, an empty chair or a bright window can all draw attention. What matters depends on the story.
Balance and empty space
An image can look balanced without being perfectly symmetrical. Empty space—sometimes called negative space—may make a subject feel isolated, or simply show where the subject is looking.
The rule of thirds is a tool

A common guide divides the frame into three rows and three columns. Placing a subject near those lines is one option, not a rule that makes all shots better. Centered compositions can be just as effective.
lessons.idea: Composition is about choosing what viewers notice and how visual elements relate to one another.
lessons.q: What is the rule of thirds?
opts: A useful composition guide, not a requirement
A rule every good film must follow
A rule about filming exactly three people
lessons.feedback: Thirds are optional guides. Centered and other compositions can work beautifully.
lessons.try: Take two photographs of the same object: centered, then toward one side. What changes?

lessons.title: When the camera moves
lessons.subtitle: Learn the basic difference between pan, tilt and moving position.
sections: Pan and tilt
A pan turns the camera side-to-side from its position. A tilt turns it up or down. These are rotations of camera direction, not necessarily moves to a new camera position.
Moving through space
A tracking or dolly movement changes the camera’s position. It can follow a character, reveal surroundings or change relationships between foreground and background. The equipment can vary.
Move for a reason

A stationary shot can be more useful than a moving one. Ask: what new information or feeling might the movement bring? A shaky image is not automatically realistic, and a smooth image is not automatically good.
lessons.idea: Camera direction and camera position are different choices, and both can change what a viewer sees.
lessons.q: Which description is correct?
opts: A pan always moves the camera to a different location
A pan rotates the camera sideways; a tracking move changes camera position
A zoom and a tracking move always look identical
lessons.feedback: Pan refers to rotating the camera sideways; a tracking move changes its location.
lessons.try: Record a still view, then a slow side-to-side pan. Compare what viewers discover.

lessons.title: What do lenses change?
lessons.subtitle: Field of view, camera distance and the look of space.
sections: How much fits in the picture
On the same camera sensor, a shorter focal-length lens generally shows a wider field of view than a longer one. Other factors, including sensor size and camera position, also matter.
Where the camera stands matters

Perspective—how nearby and distant objects appear in relation to one another—depends mainly on the camera’s position. Merely cropping or zooming an image from the same position does not produce the same perspective shift as moving the camera.
A practical first experiment

Take one photo from your position, then step closer and take another. Compare the size relationship between the subject and background. Do not confuse changes caused by moving position with those caused by focal length alone.
lessons.idea: Lens choice affects field of view; camera position is crucial to perspective. Both affect the image.
lessons.q: What most directly changes perspective relationships?
opts: Changing the camera position
Changing only the playback volume
Adding a title at the end
lessons.feedback: Camera position determines perspective relationships. Focal length changes field of view on a given sensor.
lessons.try: Stand in one place and use phone zoom, then move closer and take another picture. Compare the backgrounds.

lessons.title: How colour guides attention
lessons.subtitle: Explore how colour differences change what stands out inside an image.
sections: Colour is part of the picture

A film’s colours come from many decisions: costumes, sets, light, camera capture and adjustments during post-production. A bright object against a muted background may stand out and draw the viewer’s attention.
Colour can suggest, not guarantee
Warm-looking and cool-looking palettes may suggest different settings or moods. But blue never always means sadness and red never always means danger. Meaning depends on the story and on the viewer.
Try changing one decision

Keep the same simple scene and compare a neutral, warm and cool illustration. Notice what becomes more noticeable and what feels different. This teaching exercise is not a physically accurate colour-grading tool.
lessons.idea: Colour can guide attention and support storytelling, but it has no fixed emotional dictionary.
lessons.try: Choose one coloured object for a scene and explain why it matters to the story.
lessons.q: Which statement about colour in films is accurate?
opts: Every colour has one universal emotion
Colour choices can support attention and meaning in context
Colour is decided only after shooting
lessons.feedback: Colour can come from the set, costume, lighting, photography and finishing choices.

lessons.title: Sound changes everything
lessons.subtitle: Hear how a scene can mean something different without changing the image.
sections: Sound adds information
Footsteps, traffic or a ringing phone can tell us what is happening—even when we cannot see it. Background sounds also help us imagine where a scene takes place.
Music can change a scene’s mood
Soft music might make someone waiting feel hopeful. Uneasy music might make the same wait feel frightening. These are possibilities, not guaranteed reactions.
No music is also a choice
A scene without background music can make small sounds, such as breathing or footsteps, more noticeable. No music is not always the same as complete silence.
lessons.idea: Sound can give information, suggest emotion and guide what we notice.
lessons.try: Open the Sound Lab. Compare the same imagined scene with no music, gentle tones and uneasy tones. Note what story you start imagining.
lessons.q: What can music do even if the visuals do not change?
opts: Change the emotional expectation
Change the actor’s expression in the video
Guarantee every viewer feels the same
lessons.feedback: Music can suggest a mood or raise an expectation, even when the picture stays the same.

lessons.title: Why do filmmakers cut?
lessons.subtitle: An editor chooses what we see and for how long.
sections: What is a cut?
A cut is a direct change from one shot to the next. Cuts can guide our attention, connect actions, or reveal information. A film can also use a long shot without cutting.
Order shapes information

Show a clock before a waiting person, and viewers may notice time first. Show the place first, and they learn where the person is. The order can influence understanding without guaranteeing a single reaction.
Duration changes what we can notice
Holding a shot longer can give us more time to observe it. A quick change may draw attention to a new detail. The pacing that works depends on the action and the story.
lessons.idea: Editing arranges shots in time, and both order and duration can affect what viewers notice.
lessons.try: Use the Cut Lab. Rearrange three shots and change how long one shot stays visible.
lessons.q: Which is a creative decision made during editing?
opts: The order and duration of shots
Only the number of expensive lights
Making every scene exactly 20 seconds
lessons.feedback: Editors often choose which shots appear, their order and their duration.

lessons.title: Dialogue and the world of sound
lessons.subtitle: A scene can feel alive even without music.
sections: Listen beyond the dialogue
A film soundtrack may contain speech, effects, atmosphere and music. Footsteps, traffic and wind can help us imagine a space without the camera showing every source.
What is ambience?

Ambience is background sound that helps establish a place or atmosphere, such as distant traffic or insects. “Room tone” is typically a recording of the background sound of a filming space, useful in editing. The terms are related but not always interchangeable.
Make words understandable

During a beginner shoot, protect clear speech: avoid loud unwanted noise, bring the microphone closer when practical and check a short test recording. Sound recorded badly may be difficult to repair later.
lessons.idea: Dialogue, environmental sound and silence are storytelling tools—not just decorations around music.
lessons.q: Which statement about a film soundtrack is true?
opts: Soundtrack always means background songs only
Dialogue, effects and ambience can be part of the soundtrack
A scene with no music has no sound
lessons.feedback: The soundtrack includes many audio elements; music is only one possible part.
lessons.try: Record 10 seconds in your room. Listen for sounds you had not consciously noticed.

lessons.title: How music changes a scene
lessons.subtitle: Learn how sound can guide expectations without controlling everyone.
sections: Same image, different expectations
A character walking home can seem peaceful with gentle music—or uneasy with dissonant tones. But viewers do not all respond in exactly the same way.
Music inside or outside the scene

Music from a radio that characters can hear is often called diegetic music. Music added for the audience that characters do not hear is often called non-diegetic score. Filmmakers can blur these boundaries creatively.
Know when to stop
Silence or ordinary environmental sounds may work better than music in some moments. Music needs permission to use unless it is your own or appropriately licensed.
lessons.idea: Music can influence pacing, expectation and emotion, but the whole scene gives it meaning.
lessons.q: What is an example of diegetic music?
opts: A radio playing in the fictional room, heard by the characters
An orchestral score that only the audience hears
The picture fading to black
lessons.feedback: Diegetic music belongs to the story world, such as a radio heard by characters.
lessons.try: Watch your own short recording with no music, then with a licensed or original simple melody. What shifts?

lessons.title: Make separate shots feel connected
lessons.subtitle: Help viewers follow action and space when a scene cuts between images.
sections: What is continuity?

Imagine a character places a cup on the left side of a table. A moment later, the scene cuts to another view and the cup is suddenly on the right, although nobody moved it. The unexpected change may distract viewers.
Keep the important details clear

Filmmakers check positions, props, costume details, movement, eye-lines and sound across shots. Editing can also carry an action across a cut. Continuity is about helping viewers understand what happened, not making all images identical.
Breaking continuity can be deliberate

A sudden change may be purposeful in a dream, montage or unusual style. The question is whether the change helps the story or only confuses the viewer. Try the Continuity Lab and decide which change needs an explanation.
lessons.idea: Continuity helps the audience understand connected action across different shots.
lessons.try: Film somebody picking up a pen twice from two framings. Try joining the action at the same point.
lessons.q: Why do filmmakers usually watch continuity?
opts: To make sure nothing ever changes in the story
To keep actions, positions and story information understandable across cuts
To avoid using more than one camera position
lessons.feedback: A continuity match helps separate recorded views feel connected.

lessons.title: How editing creates rhythm
lessons.subtitle: Study the effect of how long each image stays on screen.
sections: Duration matters
If a shot lasts one second, viewers have less time to look around than if it lasts five seconds. Editors choose durations in relation to action, information, performance, dialogue and other shots.
Rhythm is not just fast cutting

A scene may feel quick because the action moves rapidly, or slow because an important moment is held. Long shots can be tense; short shots can feel calm in some contexts. The surrounding film changes how each choice works.
Transitions are choices, too

A cut is an immediate switch between shots. A dissolve briefly blends one image into another. Neither is automatically more professional. Their purpose matters more than adding effects. Use the Cut Lab to adjust shot order and time.
lessons.idea: Editing rhythm comes from relationships among duration, movement, sound and story information.
lessons.try: Make two versions of three photos: one with one-second holds, one with four-second holds.
lessons.q: What can change when an editor lengthens a shot?
opts: Viewers may have more time to notice details
The story must become sad
The camera has to use a longer lens
lessons.feedback: Duration affects viewing time, but the emotional effect depends on context.

lessons.title: Who actually makes a film?
lessons.subtitle: Understand the creative teamwork behind every scene.
sections: Films often need teamwork
Many films are made by teams. One person may write, another may perform, while others handle camera, lighting, sound, sets and editing. On a very small film, one person might do several jobs.
One scene, many jobs

In a rainy-night scene, the design team might prepare the setting, the camera and lighting teams decide how it looks, and the sound team records or creates what we hear. The editor chooses which shots appear and for how long. The director works with these people on the overall scene.
What are the “24 crafts”?

In the Telugu film industry, “24 crafts” commonly refers to 24 categories of film workers represented by industry groups. It does not mean every film worldwide has exactly 24 jobs. We will start by meeting nine familiar roles and teams.
lessons.idea: Different film jobs support one another. Working together can make a scene clearer and more powerful.
lessons.try: Think of a film scene you love. Identify three different crafts that must have contributed to it.
lessons.q: Who can contribute to how a scene feels?
opts: Only the director
Only the cinematographer
Multiple collaborating departments
lessons.feedback: Many people can shape a scene. On a small project, one person may also do several jobs.

lessons.title: What are the Indian 24 crafts?
lessons.subtitle: Understand the Telugu industry term without confusing it with a worldwide job list.
sections: What the phrase means

In the Telugu film industry, “24 crafts” commonly refers to 24 categories of film workers represented through industry associations and federation arrangements. It does not mean that every production has exactly 24 jobs, or that all countries use the same categories.
Many kinds of workers make cinema

A film may need people handling sets, camera work, lighting, costumes, makeup, sound, transport, editing and many other tasks. Some categories refer to workers or unions rather than a single creative title. The exact organization depends on the production and industry.
Respect collaboration

On a small independent shoot, one person may perform several jobs. Large productions can have many specialists. No craft is unimportant just because its workers work behind the camera. We are teaching the context here, not claiming a verified official list of all 24 association names.
lessons.idea: The “24 crafts” label describes a Telugu film-industry worker/federation context, not a universal set of 24 fixed creative jobs.
lessons.try: Choose one behind-the-scenes task you had not thought about before. How could it affect a scene?
lessons.q: Which claim about the Telugu 24 crafts is correct?
opts: Every film worldwide has exactly 24 jobs
The term is associated with Telugu film-industry worker categories
The crafts only refer to actors and directors
lessons.feedback: This is an industry-specific worker grouping, and the number of people/roles varies by film.

lessons.title: How departments plan one scene
lessons.subtitle: Watch writing, art, camera and sound decisions connect.
sections: Start from the story
Imagine a child returns home and finds an empty dinner table. The writer may describe this action. The director and team then decide how to stage and communicate the moment.
Different crafts shape one image

The production-design team may dress the table. Costume and makeup help create the people we see. Camera and lighting teams decide what is visible and how it is recorded. Actors bring their interpretation to the action.
Images and sound meet in the edit

The sound team records dialogue and other useful sounds. The editor selects and arranges recorded material with the director. Teams overlap in practice and work together rather than in one rigid chain.
lessons.idea: Creative and technical departments collaborate; changes in one department can affect the others.
lessons.try: Pick an object from the dinner-table scene. What would writing, art, camera and sound each decide?
lessons.q: Who can influence the way a filmed dinner table appears?
opts: Only the director
Only the camera operator
Several departments working together
lessons.feedback: Writing, direction, performance, design, lighting and camera choices can all affect the result.

lessons.title: From first idea to finished film
lessons.subtitle: See the basic stages of a production and what can change along the way.
sections: Develop and prepare
Development includes shaping a story, writing and finding support. Pre-production is the practical preparation: casting, locations, schedules, crew, equipment and deciding what to film.
Film the material

Production usually includes principal photography: recording performances, images and location sound. A crew may repeat takes, change plans or discover a better idea during filming. Safety and clear communication matter.
Finish and share

Post-production can include editing, sound editing, effects, music, colour finishing and final output. Distribution is how audiences get to see the film, such as festivals, cinemas or online services. These stages can overlap.
lessons.idea: Film production often moves through development, preparation, shooting, finishing and distribution, with some overlap.
lessons.try: Draw five boxes for your own tiny film. Add one task to each box.
lessons.q: When are actors and scenes typically recorded on camera?
opts: Usually during production/principal photography
Only during distribution
Only after the film is released
lessons.feedback: Principal photography is generally part of production, before the final edit is complete.

lessons.title: From idea to first film
lessons.subtitle: The simple journey from a thought to something people can watch.
sections: Plan a small story
Choose a simple idea. Who is in it? What do they want? Where does it happen? Write a short script (a plan for what people do and say), choose a place and list the shots you need.
Record your shots

You can start with a phone and a quiet place. Film the actions you need from one or more useful angles. Try to keep small details—like where an object sits—the same between matching shots. Check that voices can be heard clearly.
Put the film together
Choose your recorded shots and place them in order. Decide where to cut. Use sound or music you made yourself or have permission to use. Show the result to someone and ask what they understood.
lessons.idea: Make one short, complete film. Watch it, learn one thing and try again.
lessons.try: Make a 30-second film about someone discovering an unexpected message. Use five shots or fewer.
lessons.q: What is a sensible first film project for a beginner?
opts: A feature film with 30 locations
A short story you can finish with a few shots
A film that requires expensive cameras
lessons.feedback: A small project is easier to finish, review and learn from.

lessons.title: Plan shots before you shoot
lessons.subtitle: A simple shot list can save time and missed details.
sections: A shot list is a filming plan
A shot list records the shots you intend to capture, often with shot size, action and any notes the crew needs. It is about what you plan to record—not necessarily the order the final film will use.
A storyboard uses pictures
A storyboard sketches possible images to help plan a scene. A shot list uses written details; the two tools can work together. Neither guarantees what the finished edit will look like.
Keep your first plan short
For a tiny scene, try a wider view of the location, an action and an important reaction. Record more or change the plan when the story requires it; there is no universal three-shot rule.
lessons.idea: A shot list helps plan what to record; an editor later decides how recorded material becomes the final sequence.
lessons.q: What is the main purpose of a shot list?
opts: To list shots you plan to film
To set the final order of every film forever
To replace all conversations between crew members
lessons.feedback: A shot list helps the shoot. The final edit can use a different order or fewer/more shots.
lessons.try: Use Make Lab to plan three shots and export a shot list. Then try filming them on a phone.

lessons.title: Shoot a small scene with a phone
lessons.subtitle: Prepare one manageable moment and capture the images and sound.
sections: Keep the idea possible
Choose one place, one simple action and somebody willing to act. For example, a character finds a note and decides whether to open it. Make sure you have permission to film people and locations.
Plan what the audience needs

Sketch a wider view, a useful action detail and a reaction if the story calls for them. These are possible choices, not a requirement for exactly three shots. Check light and sound before recording, hold the phone steady when useful, and avoid unsafe filming.
Record and check

Record enough of the action to allow editing. Repeat a take if needed and check that speech is understandable. Watch or listen to the recordings before leaving the location so missing action or sound can be captured again.
lessons.idea: A small clear idea, safe preparation and usable sound matter more than expensive equipment.
lessons.try: Use Make Lab to export a simple plan; then record one 10–30-second moment on your phone.
lessons.q: Which is a useful habit while shooting a first scene?
opts: Record everything without checking sound
Review important recordings before leaving
Always use exactly three shots
lessons.feedback: Checking image and sound on location can reveal problems while they can still be fixed.

lessons.title: Edit a short story from your shots
lessons.subtitle: Turn recorded clips into a beginning, middle and ending.
sections: Choose what helps the story
First select usable recordings. Place them in an order the audience can follow. You can remove repetition and change the length of each part. An editor does not have to use every recorded take.
Hear the joins

Listen through each edit for abrupt changes in background sound or important dialogue. A clear consistent sound bed may help a sequence feel connected. Adding music is optional; avoid using music you do not have rights to share.
Finish a simple version

Make a first cut around 30–60 seconds. The story does not have to be exactly one minute. Watch it without stopping and ask whether the main action is understandable. Export it in a suitable format for the device or platform where it will be viewed.
lessons.idea: Editing is choosing and arranging recorded material to communicate the story clearly.
lessons.try: Open Cut Lab and create two different three-shot timings, then try a similar edit in a real editor.
lessons.q: What should guide which takes an editor selects?
opts: Whether they support the intended scene
Whether they were recorded first
Whether every take can be used
lessons.feedback: An editor chooses material for performance, clarity, continuity and storytelling needs.

lessons.title: Watch, learn and improve
lessons.subtitle: Learn from your first film without treating creativity as a pass/fail formula.
sections: Watch like a new viewer
Show a rough cut to someone who does not know the story, if they agree. Ask what they understood and where they became confused. Do not explain the scene first; observe their reaction.
Ask focused questions

Could they understand the character’s action? Was speech audible? Could they tell where events happened? Was a visual clue hard to notice? These questions can identify problems you can actually improve.
Make one useful revision

Change one thing at a time: a cut, an audio level, a missing close view or a title. Different people may prefer different artistic choices. Learn from the feedback, but keep your reason for making the film in mind.
lessons.idea: Useful critique asks what a film communicates and how its choices work, not simply whether someone likes it.
lessons.try: Write two questions you want a viewer to answer about your one-minute film.
lessons.q: Which feedback is most helpful for revising a beginner film?
opts: “The film is bad.”
“I could not hear the key line at 20 seconds.”
“All films should use close-ups.”
lessons.feedback: Specific observations help you decide what to improve, even if you keep a creative choice.

teluguNotes.why: సినిమాలు మనకు వినోదం, సమాచారం, కొత్త అనుభవాలు ఇవ్వవచ్చు. డాక్యుమెంటరీలు నిజ జీవిత విషయాలను కూడా చూపిస్తాయి. ఒకే సన్నివేశాన్ని చూసిన ఇద్దరూ ఒకేలా స్పందించాల్సిన అవసరం లేదు.
teluguNotes.units: ఫ్రేమ్ (Frame) అంటే వీడియోలోని ఒక్క చిత్రం. షాట్ (Shot) అంటే పూర్తయిన సినిమాలో మధ్యలో కట్ లేకుండా కనిపించే ఒక దృశ్య భాగం. సీన్ (Scene) అంటే కథలోని ఒక భాగం; అందులో ఒకటి లేదా అనేక షాట్లు ఉండవచ్చు. టేక్ (Take) అంటే షాట్‌ను రికార్డ్ చేయడానికి చేసిన ఒక ప్రయత్నం.
teluguNotes.shot: షాట్ అందంగా కనిపించడం మాత్రమే ముఖ్యం కాదు. ఆ క్షణంలో ప్రేక్షకులు ఏం గమనించాలి లేదా అర్థం చేసుకోవాలి అనేది ఆలోచించాలి. వైడ్ షాట్ (Wide shot), క్లోజప్ (Close-up) లాంటి ఎంపికల అర్థం కథ సందర్భాన్ని బట్టి మారుతుంది.
teluguNotes.story: పాత్రకు ఏం కావాలి? అది ఎందుకు ముఖ్యం? దానికి అడ్డంకి ఏమిటి? ఇవి కథపై ఆసక్తిని పెంచగల ప్రశ్నలు. కానీ ప్రతి కథ ఒకే పద్ధతిలో ఉండాల్సిన అవసరం లేదు.
teluguNotes.crew: సినిమాలో రచన, దర్శకత్వం, నటన, కెమెరా, సౌండ్, ఎడిటింగ్ లాంటి పనులు కలిసి పనిచేస్తాయి. చిన్న సినిమాలో ఒకరే అనేక పనులు చేయవచ్చు. తెలుగు చిత్ర పరిశ్రమలో “24 క్రాఫ్ట్స్” అనేది కార్మికుల వృత్తి విభాగాలకు సంబంధించిన పదం; ప్రపంచమంతటికీ ఒకే జాబితా కాదు.
teluguNotes.sound: సౌండ్ (Sound) అంటే సంగీతం మాత్రమే కాదు. మాటలు, అడుగుల చప్పుడు, వాతావరణంలోని శబ్దాలు కూడా ఇందులో భాగమే. సంగీతం లేకున్నా ఇతర శబ్దాలు ఉండవచ్చు. ఏ శబ్దం ఎలాంటి భావనను కలిగిస్తుందో సన్నివేశంపై ఆధారపడుతుంది.
teluguNotes.camera: కెమెరాను ఎక్కడ ఉంచుతామో దానివల్ల ప్రేక్షకులు చూసే వివరాలు మారవచ్చు. కింద నుంచి తీసిన షాట్ ఎప్పుడూ శక్తిని చూపదు; పై నుంచి తీసిన షాట్ ఎప్పుడూ బలహీనతను చూపదు. కెమెరా కోణం (Angle) అర్థం సన్నివేశాన్ని బట్టి మారుతుంది.
teluguNotes.history: సినిమా ఒక్క రోజులో, ఒక్క వ్యక్తి వల్ల పుట్టలేదు. కెమెరా, కదిలే చిత్రాలు, ప్రొజెక్షన్ వంటి పద్ధతులను చాలామంది అభివృద్ధి చేశారు. 1895 పారిస్ ప్రదర్శన ముఖ్యమైన ఘట్టం, కానీ దానికంటే ముందే ఇతర ప్రదర్శనలు జరిగాయి.
teluguNotes.script: ఐడియాను చిత్రీకరించగల చర్యలుగా రాయడంలో స్క్రీన్‌ప్లే (Screenplay) సహాయపడుతుంది. పాత్ర ఏం చేస్తుంది, ఏమి చెబుతుంది, కథ ఎక్కడ జరుగుతుంది అనే విషయాలు ఇందులో ఉండవచ్చు.
teluguNotes.acting: నటులు మాటలతో పాటు చూపులు, కదలికలు, విరామాలు, స్వరం ద్వారా కూడా పాత్రను చూపిస్తారు. నటనకు అర్థం సన్నివేశాన్ని బట్టి మారుతుంది.
teluguNotes.lighting: లైటింగ్ (Lighting) వల్ల ముఖం, వస్తువులు, నీడలు ఎలా కనిపిస్తాయో మారుతుంది. కాంతి దిశ, పరిమాణం, దూరం, బలం ప్రభావం చూపవచ్చు. ఒక్క విధమైన లైట్‌కు ఒక్క భావమే ఉండదు.
teluguNotes.editing: ఎడిటింగ్ (Editing)లో షాట్లను ఎంచుకొని క్రమంలో పెడతారు. కట్ (Cut) అంటే ఒక షాట్ నుంచి మరో షాట్‌కు నేరుగా మారడం. ఏ షాట్‌ను ఎంతసేపు చూపిస్తామన్నదీ ముఖ్యం.
teluguNotes.making: చిన్న ఐడియాతో మొదలుపెట్టండి. పాత్ర ఎవరు? వాళ్లకు ఏం కావాలి? కథ ఎక్కడ జరుగుతుంది? ముందుగా ప్లాన్ చేసి, ఫోన్‌తో అవసరమైన షాట్లు తీయండి. మాటలు స్పష్టంగా వినిపిస్తున్నాయో చూసుకోండి. షాట్లను క్రమంలో పెట్టి చిన్న సినిమా పూర్తి చేయండి.
teluguNotes.genres: జానర్ (Genre) అంటే కథల లక్షణాలను బట్టి ఇచ్చే పేరు. కామెడీ, హారర్, మిస్టరీ లాంటివి ఒకే సినిమాలో కలిసివుండవచ్చు. డాక్యుమెంటరీలు నిజమైన విషయాలపై ఉన్నా, వాటిని చిత్రీకరించి ఎడిట్ చేసే నిర్ణయాలు ఉంటాయి.
teluguNotes.india: 1896లో బొంబాయిలో కదిలే చిత్రాల ప్రదర్శనలు జరిగాయి. 1912 నాటి శ్రీ పుండలిక్, 1913 నాటి రాజా హరిశ్చంద్ర ప్రారంభ భారతీయ సినిమా చరిత్రలో ముఖ్యమైనవి. “మొదటి చిత్రం” అనే విషయంపై చరిత్రకారుల్లో చర్చ ఉంది. భారతదేశంలో ఎన్నో భాషల్లో సినిమాలు అభివృద్ధి చెందాయి.
teluguNotes.character: కథలో పాత్రకు ఏం కావాలి, దానికి ఏది అడ్డుగా ఉంది, ఆ పాత్ర ఏం నిర్ణయం తీసుకుంటుంది అనే ప్రశ్నలు కథను ముందుకు నడిపించవచ్చు. ప్రతి అడ్డంకి గొడవే కావాల్సిన అవసరం లేదు.
teluguNotes.dialogue: డైలాగ్ అంటే పాత్ర మాట్లాడే మాటలు. మాటలతో పాటు స్వరం, చూపు, నిశ్శబ్దం కూడా అర్థాన్ని మార్చవచ్చు. నేరుగా చెప్పకుండా సందర్భం ద్వారా అర్థమయ్యే భావాన్ని సబ్‌టెక్స్ట్ (Subtext) అంటారు.
teluguNotes.composition: ఫ్రేమ్ లో వ్యక్తులు, వస్తువులు, ఖాళీ స్థలం ఎలా అమర్చారో అదే కంపోజిషన్. రూల్ ఆఫ్ థర్డ్స్ ఒక ఉపయోగకరమైన సూచన మాత్రమే; ప్రతి మంచి షాట్ దాన్నే పాటించాల్సిన అవసరం లేదు.
teluguNotes.movement: పాన్ (Pan)లో కెమెరా ఒకే స్థానం నుంచి పక్కలకు తిరుగుతుంది. టిల్ట్ (Tilt)లో పైకి లేదా కిందికి తిరుగుతుంది. ట్రాకింగ్ షాట్‌లో కెమెరా ఉన్న స్థానం మారుతుంది. కదలికకు కథలో కారణం ఉండటం ఉపయోగకరం.
teluguNotes.lenses: అదే సెన్సార్‌పై తక్కువ ఫోకల్ లెంగ్త్ ఉన్న లెన్స్ సాధారణంగా ఎక్కువ ప్రాంతాన్ని చూపిస్తుంది. దగ్గర, దూరం వస్తువులు ఎలా కనిపిస్తాయనే పర్స్పెక్టివ్‌కు కెమెరా ఉన్న స్థానం చాలా ముఖ్యం.
teluguNotes.ambience: సినిమాలో మాటలు, అడుగుల శబ్దం, వాతావరణ శబ్దాలు, సంగీతం ఉంటాయి. ఆంబియెన్స్ (Ambience) స్థలానికి సంబంధించిన నేపథ్య శబ్దం. రూమ్ టోన్ (Room tone) ఎడిటింగ్‌కు ఉపయోగపడే ప్రదేశపు నేపథ్య శబ్ద రికార్డింగ్.
teluguNotes.music: అదే సన్నివేశానికి సంగీతం మార్చితే ప్రేక్షకుల అంచనాలు మారవచ్చు. పాత్రకు కూడా వినిపించే రేడియో సంగీతాన్ని డైజెటిక్ (Diegetic) మ్యూజిక్ అనవచ్చు. సంగీతం లేకపోయినా సౌండ్ ఉండవచ్చు.
teluguNotes.shotlist: షాట్ లిస్ట్ (Shot list) అంటే చిత్రీకరించాలని ప్లాన్ చేసిన షాట్ల జాబితా. స్టోరీబోర్డ్ (Storyboard) వాటిని చిత్రాలుగా చూపించే ప్లాన్. ఎడిటింగ్‌లో షాట్ల క్రమం మారవచ్చు.
teluguNotes.showdonttell: భావాన్ని పాత్ర చేసే పనితో కూడా చూపించవచ్చు. కానీ డైలాగ్ చెడ్డది కాదు. మాటలు, చూపులు, చర్యలు కలిసి కథ చెప్పగలవు. ఏది స్పష్టంగా ఉంటుందో దాన్ని ఎంచుకోండి.
teluguNotes.colour: సినిమాలో రంగులు ప్రేక్షకుల దృష్టిని ఆకర్షించవచ్చు. సెట్లు, దుస్తులు, లైటింగ్, కెమెరా, కలర్ ఫినిషింగ్ అన్నీ ప్రభావం చూపుతాయి. ఒక్క రంగుకు ఎప్పుడూ ఒకే అర్థం ఉండదు.
teluguNotes.continuity: ఒక షాట్‌లో కప్పు ఎడమ వైపు ఉంటే, తర్వాత షాట్‌లో కారణం లేకుండా కుడివైపు మారితే ప్రేక్షకులకు గందరగోళం రావచ్చు. చర్యలు, వస్తువులు, శబ్దాలు షాట్ల మధ్య అర్థమయ్యేలా ఉండడమే కంటిన్యుటీ.
teluguNotes.rhythm: షాట్ ఎంతసేపు కనిపిస్తుందో ప్రేక్షకులు వివరాలు గమనించే సమయాన్ని మార్చవచ్చు. వేగంగా కట్ చేయడమే రిథమ్ కాదు. పాత్ర చర్యలు, శబ్దాలు, కథ సందర్భం కూడా ముఖ్యం.
teluguNotes.craft24: తెలుగు సినీ పరిశ్రమలో “24 క్రాఫ్ట్స్” అనే మాట కార్మికుల వృత్తి విభాగాలు, సంఘాల సందర్భంలో వాడతారు. ప్రపంచంలోని అన్ని సినిమాల్లో కచ్చితంగా 24 ఉద్యోగాలుంటాయని అర్థం కాదు.
teluguNotes.teams: ఒక చిన్న సన్నివేశం కోసం రచన, దర్శకత్వం, నటన, కళా విభాగం, కెమెరా, లైటింగ్, సౌండ్, ఎడిటింగ్ బృందాలు పరస్పరం కలిసి పని చేయవచ్చు.
teluguNotes.pipeline: సినిమా నిర్మాణంలో కథ అభివృద్ధి, ముందస్తు ప్రణాళిక, షూటింగ్, ఎడిటింగ్ మరియు ఇతర పూర్తి చేసే పనులు, ప్రేక్షకులకు చేరవేయడం వంటి దశలు ఉంటాయి. కొన్ని పనులు ఒకేసారి జరగవచ్చు.
teluguNotes.shootscene: మొదటి సన్నివేశానికి చిన్న ఐడియా, ఒక స్థలం, ఒక సులభమైన పని ఎంచుకోండి. షాట్ ప్లాన్ చేయండి. కెమెరా, సౌండ్ పరీక్షించండి. అవసరమైతే మళ్లీ టేక్ తీసి రికార్డింగ్ వెంటనే చూసుకోండి.
teluguNotes.editminute: ఎడిటింగ్‌లో ఉపయోగపడే టేక్‌లను ఎంచుకొని క్రమంలో పెడతారు. అవసరం లేని భాగాలు తీసేయవచ్చు. మాటలు స్పష్టంగా ఉన్నాయో, కట్‌ల మధ్య సౌండ్ సహజంగా ఉందో చూసి చిన్న కథను పూర్తి చేయండి.
teluguNotes.review: మీ చిన్న సినిమా చూసిన వ్యక్తిని కథ అర్థమైందా, ఎక్కడ సందేహం వచ్చింది, మాటలు వినిపించాయా అని అడగండి. ఉపయోగకరమైన సూచనను తీసుకుని ఒక మార్పు చేసి మళ్లీ చూడండి.

glossary.meaning: One image in a video. Pause a video to see one frame.
An uninterrupted view in the finished film, before a cut.
A part of the story, usually focused on one event or situation. It may contain several shots.
One recorded attempt at filming a shot or performance.
A direct change from one shot to another in the edit.
A shot that shows the subject and a larger part of the surroundings.
A shot that shows a person or object in greater detail.
How people, objects and other visual elements are arranged inside the frame.
A written plan for a film, including scene action and usually dialogue.
The craft of creating a film’s camera images, including framing and lighting choices.
Selecting and arranging shots, and choosing when we move between them.
Creating and shaping the sound world of a film, including effects and atmosphere.
Controlling and using light to shape how subjects and spaces appear on camera.
The direction a subject moves or faces within the image.
Maintaining understandable connections between shots, such as action, positions and time.
A principal light used to illuminate a subject in a lighting setup.
Light coming from behind a subject relative to the camera, often helping to outline its edges.
What a character could gain, lose or experience because of a choice or event.
A sound used to represent or suggest an event, object or action.
How fast or slowly events and shots seem to move through a story.
A flexible category describing shared film features or audience expectations.
A film exploring real people, events or subjects, shaped through choices in filming and editing.
An obstacle or tension that makes a character’s goal difficult.
A meaning suggested by actions or context rather than stated directly.
Open or relatively empty area around the main subject in an image.
Rotating the camera horizontally from its position.
Rotating the camera up or down from its position.
A shot in which the camera changes position through space.
A lens property that helps determine its field of view on a given sensor.
The visual relationship of near and far objects as viewed from a camera position.
Background sound that helps establish a place or atmosphere.
Background sound recorded at a location, often useful for sound editing.
Sound that belongs to the world of the story.
A written plan of shots the crew intends to record.
Drawings that plan possible images in a scene.
A selection of colours used together in the look of a film.
How strong or muted a colour appears.
Editing choices intended to make action and space easy to follow across shots.
Cutting between views while one action appears to continue.
A transition where one image gradually blends into another.
Planning and preparing a film before principal photography.
The stage that commonly includes recording the main performances and scenes.
Work after or alongside filming that helps finish a film, including editing and sound.
The main period of shooting a film’s scenes.
An early version of an edit that can be reviewed and revised.
An object used by a performer or in the action of a scene.
Objects and details arranged to make a filmed space look right for the story.

crafts.title: Screenwriting
crafts.desc: Write the story and what happens in each scene.
crafts.detail: Screenwriters plan characters, events and dialogue (what people say). Their screenplay describes what happens in the film. It is a guide for making the film, not the finished film.
crafts.link: The director works with writers, actors and other teams to turn the script into a film.

crafts.title: Directing
crafts.desc: Guide how the story is shown and performed.
crafts.detail: The director guides how the story is told on screen. They work with actors and other teams to make choices about performance, camera work, sound and editing.
crafts.link: Directing works closely with writing, acting, camera, editing and sound.

crafts.title: Cinematography
crafts.desc: Plan how the film looks through the camera.
crafts.detail: The cinematographer, also called the director of photography, plans much of the camera work and lighting with the director. They help decide how shots are framed, lit and recorded.
crafts.link: Cinematography works closely with directing, lighting and production design.

crafts.title: Acting
crafts.desc: Show what a character thinks, feels and does.
crafts.detail: Actors play characters through actions, facial expressions, movement and voice. They can show us what someone feels, even without speaking.
crafts.link: Acting connects the script and the director’s ideas to what the audience sees and hears.

crafts.title: Production Design
crafts.desc: Plan how the film’s places and sets look.
crafts.detail: The production designer leads the overall look of sets and locations on screen. They work with the art department and other teams on things like furniture, colours and the world around the characters.
crafts.link: Production design works with the director, camera and other visual teams.

crafts.title: Sound
crafts.desc: Record and shape what the audience hears.
crafts.detail: Sound workers record voices and noises during filming. Later, sound editors and designers may clean up speech, add effects and shape the background sounds we hear.
crafts.link: Sound works closely with directing, editing and music.

crafts.title: Editing
crafts.desc: Choose shots and decide when they change.
crafts.detail: The editor chooses recorded shots and arranges them in an order that makes sense. How long we see each shot, and when the film cuts, can change how a moment feels.
crafts.link: Editing works closely with the director, sound and music teams.

crafts.title: Film Music
crafts.desc: Use music to support or contrast with a scene.
crafts.detail: Composers can write original music for a film. Filmmakers may also choose existing songs if they have permission to use them. Music may suggest a feeling—or the film may work better without it.
crafts.link: Film music works with the director, editor and sound team.

crafts.title: Producing
crafts.desc: Help organize the people, money and plan.
crafts.detail: Producers help make a film happen. Their work can include finding money, hiring people, planning the schedule and helping the project reach an audience. Different producers handle different parts of this work.
crafts.link: Producing helps the creative teams get the resources and support they need.

why.prompt: A person waits at an empty bus stop. What could start your film?
opts: The empty bench
The location and empty space become important first.
The waiting face
The viewer may start by studying the character’s response.

history.prompt: You can record a short moment from daily life. What will you show?
opts: People leaving work
An everyday event can become an interesting moving image.
A staged surprise
Even a short staged action can tell a miniature story.

units.prompt: You film the same short action three times. What do you have?
opts: Three takes
Yes. Each recording attempt can be called a take.
Three scenes
Not necessarily. Repeating one action does not automatically create three scenes.

story.prompt: Your character needs a key. What makes the search matter?
opts: We know what it unlocks
Understanding the importance of the key can give the action stakes.
Show only close-ups
Framing can focus attention, but by itself does not explain why the key matters.

script.prompt: You need to show nervousness in a script. Which line can be filmed directly?
opts: She avoids the letter
That describes an action actors can perform; what it means depends on context.
Her soul feels anxious
This may describe an intention, but the team still needs choices that viewers can see or hear.

acting.prompt: Your character hears surprising news. How might an actor respond?
opts: Pause before speaking
A pause can show that the character is taking in the news.
Speak immediately
An instant response might suggest urgency or certainty. Either can work in context.

shot.prompt: A character is alone in a large station. What do you show first?
opts: The whole station
A wide view can establish the space and the character within it.
Their face
A closer view can focus attention on the character before revealing the setting.

camera.prompt: You want to reveal what is behind a character. What could you try?
opts: Move the camera
Camera movement can gradually reveal what was hidden.
Cut to another view
Editing to a new shot can also reveal the information.

lighting.prompt: You want viewers to notice the side of a face. What might help?
opts: A side light
Side lighting can create visible differences between lit and shadowed areas.
A front light
Front lighting may reveal more facial detail with less side-to-side contrast.

sound.prompt: A hallway looks empty. Which audio choice do you test?
opts: Footsteps out of view
That sound can suggest somebody is nearby without showing them.
No background music
Without music, other sounds or quiet can become more noticeable.

editing.prompt: You have a clock and a waiting person. Which comes first?
opts: The clock
That may make time feel relevant before we meet the character.
The person
That may direct attention to the person before revealing the clock.

crew.prompt: A night scene is difficult to read. Who could help?
opts: Camera and lighting teams
They can adjust how the scene is lit and photographed.
Art and costume teams
They can also improve how characters and the setting are visually distinguished.

making.prompt: Your first short needs ten locations. What is worth trying?
opts: Simplify to one place
A smaller scope often makes a first project more achievable.
Keep all ten places
It could work with enough planning and resources, but increases complexity.

genres.prompt: What is the genre of a story about a funny ghost?
opts: A comedy with a ghost
The ghost might be used to create humour.
A horror-comedy
The same idea could mix funny and frightening moments.

india.prompt: You are introducing Indian cinema. What should come first?
opts: One famous filmmaker
A strong example can help, but may not represent all regional histories.
Many filmmaking traditions
A multilingual introduction helps show how broad Indian cinema is.

character.prompt: A character misses the last bus. What makes it a story?
opts: They had an important appointment
The consequences may make the delay matter.
The character is afraid of going home
The internal obstacle may be more important than the bus itself.

dialogue.prompt: A character says “Welcome back.” How could it mean different things?
opts: Smile and move closer
The line might suggest warmth.
Avoid eye contact
The same words might suggest distance or discomfort.

composition.prompt: A person stands alone on a platform. How do you frame them?
opts: Place them in the center
The viewer may focus on the person immediately.
Leave room around them
The empty space may become important alongside the character.

movement.prompt: You want to follow someone turning a corner. What might you try?
opts: Pan from a fixed spot
A rotation may follow them as long as they remain in view.
Move alongside them
Moving the camera position can change the view of the surroundings.

lenses.prompt: You want more of a room in the image. What could you try?
opts: Use a shorter focal length
On the same sensor, this generally gives a wider field of view.
Move the camera backward
Changing camera position includes more space and can change perspective.

ambience.prompt: A scene takes place near a road. Which sound is worth trying?
opts: Distant traffic
Ambience can help suggest the location even off-screen.
Only the spoken lines
This focuses attention on the voices; the scene may feel different.

music.prompt: The scene is about waiting. What should be tested?
opts: Music from the character’s phone
If the character hears it, it may belong to the story world.
No added music
Existing dialogue and ambience may become easier to notice.

shotlist.prompt: Before filming, what do you choose to prepare?
opts: A small shot list
It may help you remember the actions and views needed.
Just start recording
Improvising can work, but you may discover missing shots later.

showdonttell.prompt: A character misses someone. What could introduce that idea?
opts: They speak about it
Dialogue can explain feelings directly and reveal how the person speaks.
They put away an unused cup
An observable action may invite viewers to infer absence.

colour.prompt: You want viewers to notice one letter. What might help?
opts: Contrast its colour against the desk
A noticeable difference can draw attention without defining an emotion.
Use similar colours throughout
A subtle palette may be useful, but the letter could be harder to notice.

continuity.prompt: A cup is on the left of a table. The next shot shows it on the right. What do you do?
opts: Check whether someone moved it
If the story did not show a move, the sudden change might distract viewers.
Keep the mismatch deliberately
A deliberate discontinuity can be meaningful if it serves the scene.

rhythm.prompt: A person reads a difficult letter. How long would you hold their reaction?
opts: A brief glimpse
A short duration offers less time to study the face.
A longer look
A longer duration may encourage viewers to examine the reaction.

craft24.prompt: A beginner asks: “Must my first film have 24 crew members?”
opts: No; the phrase is about worker categories
Small productions often combine roles. The federation term is not a crew-size rule.
Yes; it is a worldwide production rule
That is incorrect. Crew size and departments vary by film.

teams.prompt: A table scene looks too empty. Who might help?
opts: Art/set dressing and camera teams
Props, space and framing can change how the table appears.
Only the screenwriter
A script can describe the table, but a visual scene involves many collaborators.

pipeline.prompt: You are finding a location before a shoot. What stage is this normally?
opts: Pre-production
Location planning is commonly part of preparation.
Distribution
Distribution is how the finished film reaches audiences.

shootscene.prompt: You recorded a scene but cannot understand its speech. Next step?
opts: Check and record it again while possible
Catching sound problems on location can save a project.
Assume editing will fix every sound problem
Some unclear or clipped recordings cannot be repaired convincingly.

editminute.prompt: Your first rough cut has a repeating action. What could you try?
opts: Remove an unnecessary repetition
Cutting redundant material may make the action clearer.
Keep every recorded take
A finished scene does not need every take.

review.prompt: A viewer says “I did not understand what the note said.” How should you respond?
opts: Find out where clarity was lost
You can consider a better angle, edit or sound cue to explain what matters.
Tell them they watched it incorrectly
Different viewers bring valuable observations; you can still choose what to change.
